title: The whole-effect check: what an AI agent does for any initiative that asks — six hats
question: An initiative asks an AI agent to check the whole effect of what it is doing. Starting from the present, with no blame assigned, what exactly does the agent do, step by step, to trace hidden costs and indirect effects, compare ownership arrangements and propose the small move that can be undone, so that the result is more possibilities for all and less to none, and what does the one page it hands back look like?

budget.setBy: set by Tom through Watson: same engine, cap about $5

stopReason: the hat sequence ran to its close; critic passed the checkpoint

opening.question: Starting from today and blaming no one, what ordered steps does an AI agent take, using only public information and what an initiative hands over, to trace unpaid costs and knock-on effects, compare ownership arrangements and propose one reversible change, and what does the one phone-readable page it returns look like for any kind of initiative?
opening.text: We are turning a five-part draft into an ordered procedure and a one-page layout that any initiative could read on a phone and say yes or no to. We test every idea on at least three different kinds of initiative, such as a community energy scheme, a repair network and a wellbeing budget. We check facts first where the note admits it does not know, then look for value, risks to the design, and other ways to build it. We finish by naming the step an agent starts tomorrow.

white.reason: Four open unknowns, none checked: about four research loops on whether knock-on effects can be traced from public information, what evidence exists on ownership arrangements, and whether a page with no score gets used, plus one round.

black.reason: Three to four rounds on how the page could harm the initiative, people named in it or people left out, and on where tracing must stop; these are risks to the design only.

green.reason: Four rounds to try other step orders and page layouts and settle the final procedure, the page, and the first step, since the product is built here.

Results are dicts in a list; the earlier error was from my indexing. Retry.I only checked one of the three areas against its source, because my search tool hit its usage limit partway through. The rest of the list below comes from general knowledge and is unchecked.

**Community energy (checked for the UK sector report; the rest is unchecked)**
- **Sector-wide report:** Community Energy England, Community Energy Wales and Community Energy Scotland produce the annual *State of the Sector* report. It has appeared annually since 2017. The 2025 edition is dated 17 September 2025 and is a PDF on the Community Energy England publications page. It is built from survey responses, so it covers only the groups that answered.
- **Individual schemes:** Most UK schemes are registered as community benefit societies, a legal form for businesses that serve a community. As I understand it, these file annual accounts and an annual return with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Mutuals Public Register. Many also publish an annual report, a community benefit fund report and a share offer document. Member numbers usually appear in the annual return or in the scheme's own report. I did not open the register, so confirm the filing details there.

**Repair and reuse networks (unchecked)**
- Repair Café International and the Restart Project each publish their own reports. I'd expect Repair Café International to publish network counts and repair statistics, and the Restart Project to publish impact reports and repair-data reports. I did not confirm any specific document.
- Local groups are often informal and may publish nothing beyond event counts. Where a group is a registered charity or a community interest company, it files accounts with the charity or company regulator.

**Wellbeing budgets (unchecked)**
- **New Zealand:** The Treasury publishes the Budget documents and a wellbeing report. I did not verify the titles or whether the current government still publishes them.
- **Wales:** I expect the Future Generations Commissioner and public bodies to publish well-being objectives and annual reports. I did not verify this.
- **Other governments:** Check each government's own finance ministry or statistics site.

I did not find or confirm the following:
- A single standard set of documents for any of the three areas.
- Any figure on how many schemes actually publish impact reports.

items.full:
Yes, there is published comparative research, but it is uneven. It is strong on commons design and on private versus public, and thin on trusts and cooperatives.

- **Commons (Ostrom tradition):** Cox, Arnold and Villamayor's review is a meta-analysis of 91 studies that applied Ostrom's design principles to local self-governance of common-pool resources. It re-tests which institutional features go with durable management. A later paper (Sustainability 2017) applies the principles to case studies worldwide and lists factors in success and failure. I saw search-result excerpts of both, not the full papers.
- **Forest commons across regimes:** Chhatre and Agrawal's work on forest commons covers livelihoods, carbon storage and biodiversity. The excerpt I saw says forest commons are about 18% of global forest area. I did not open the paper, so I can't confirm its sample size or its specific findings on tenure types.
- **Private versus public:** Araral's meta-analysis of international experience with water-utility privatization tests the efficiency hypothesis for private ownership. I saw only the excerpt, not the findings. I recall, but did not check, that Bel, Fageda and Warner (2010) found no systematic cost difference between private and public provision of water and waste services.
- **Coverage gaps:** What I opened is mostly water, forests, irrigation and pastures. I found no cross-resource study that puts private, public, commons, trust and cooperative arrangements side by side for the same resource. Trusts and cooperatives mostly appear in single-case or sector-specific work, which I did not search for.
- **Main limits:** The commons studies are mainly case-based, so they are vulnerable to selection bias. Outcome measures differ between studies: cost efficiency, resource condition, equity and livelihoods. For the note, the claim to make is that ownership matters less than the rules in use, such as monitoring, sanctions and local rule-making. That is a reading of Ostrom's design-principles findings, not a result I checked.

I ran four searches (Ostrom meta-analyses, design principles, forest commons, water privatization) and opened none of the full papers.

**Repair Café International (the umbrella foundation, repaircafe.org)**
- **Annual reports.** They are posted in a category archive on the site. The reports include an estimate of waste prevented. The 2016 report estimated nearly 250,000 kilos of waste prevented. items.line: Yes, but only in part. ISO 14044 (2006) for life-cycle assessment has no fixed number of steps. It requires the study to state its cut-off criteria (mass, energy, environmental significance) for which inputs and outputs to include and to test how they affect the result. I did not check input-output structural path analysis, which cuts off at a chosen number of supply-chain tiers, or SROI, theory of change and EU impact assessment guidance.

items.full:
r is a string apparently.The 420,000 kg figure is confirmed as an assumption-based estimate, not a measured weight. I read the Repair Café International news post about the report and the English summary PDF of the 2019 annual report. I did not open the full Dutch report.

- **The figure:** The news post of 14 December 2020 says Repair Cafés prevented an estimated 420,000 kilos of waste in 2019. It cites the annual report.
- **The inputs:** By the end of 2019 exactly 2,000 Repair Cafés were active worldwide. A typical one has one repair meeting per month, at which an average of 25 objects are examined. On average 70 percent of these repairs are successful.
- **The calculation:** The report assumes an average object weighs 1 kg. That gives 35,000 repaired objects a month (2,000 × 25 × 0.7), or 35,000 kg a month. Over the year that is 420,000 kg.
- **Weight and count are the same number:** The English summary gives the same 420,000 as a count, saying the cafés accounted for an estimated 420,000 successful repairs. The kilogram figure therefore rests on the 1 kg-per-object assumption, with no weighing involved.
- **CO2 claim:** The report says this prevented up to 10 million kilos of CO2 emissions. That is a separate, "up to" estimate. The 2015 report said it used TNO data for its CO2 conversion. I did not check whether the 2019 report used the same method.
- **A weakness in the inputs:** The report's own RepairMonitor dataset held almost 26,000 logged repairs, and the success rate of repairs performed in 2019 was 63%. That is below the 70% used in the estimate. The 25-objects-per-meeting and one-meeting-per-month figures are assumptions applied to all 2,000 cafés. At 63%, the same arithmetic gives about 378,000 kg, roughly 10% lower. That recalculation is mine, not the report's.

items.full:
Fetch the full documents instead.No. I found no maximum number of steps of indirect effect in either document. Both instead use judgement rules (materiality and proportionality) and time limits.

- **SROI.** I read the nef/SROI Network guide, "Measuring Value" (2009, 56 pages). I searched its full text for "how far", "number of steps", "maximum" and "only include", and none of them appear. Its tool for following effects is the impact map, which follows a cause-and-effect chain from inputs to outputs, outcomes and impact. It says outcomes can arise "indirectly over time" as a result of other outcomes. It also says negative and unintended outcomes must be shown and subtracted. Its limits come from materiality ("focus on what is important") and from adjustments for deadweight, attribution, displacement and drop-off. Drop-off is a yearly decay in an outcome's value. I did not check the later Social Value UK 2012 guide.
- **EU Better Regulation Toolbox.** I read the 2023 Chapter 8 pdf on analysing impacts. Its tool on costs and benefits says to identify as many costs and benefits as possible "in a proportionate manner". It separates direct from indirect effects, and it describes indirect costs as rippling through prices in other sectors. That description has no stated depth cut-off. It notes that one category of cost is "not well-defined" and so is usually not analysed. I read only this chapter, not the rest of the toolbox.

For the note: both frameworks leave the stopping point to the analyst, so a whole-effect check would have to set its own depth rule and state it openly.

leads.text: A single page that follows costs outside the price to whoever carries them (neighbours, non-members, a later year, a river) could show an initiative harms it didn't know about, before the harm builds up.
Because it is forward-facing and blame-agnostic, an initiative may be able to read a page about its own costs without getting defensive, which could make the page more likely to be used.
Setting the current ownership arrangement beside two or three that exist elsewhere could show an initiative options it had not considered.
The small move that can be undone gives an initiative a low-risk next step with a stated way back, which may lower the cost of trying something new.
Flagging anything that could never be rebuilt might protect irreplaceable things before a decision is made.
Offering the check as a service to existing work, with no verdict or score, might make it easy to adopt across many kinds of initiative (energy, repair, land trust, company).
A page ending in questions rather than answers could prompt the initiative to use local knowledge the agent lacks.
A fixed, ordered set of steps that lets different agents produce much the same page could make the service comparable and checkable across initiatives.
Working only from public information and contacting nobody could keep the service cheap, fast, and low-risk for the people named in it.
Asking whether each turn makes the next one easier could give initiatives a way to see whether they are building lasting know-how, tools or trust.

items.text:
The design's biggest value may be that it borrows what established practice already trusts. ISO 14044, the SROI guide and EU impact guidance all ask a study to state where it stops tracing and why (R4, R6). A page that opens with one plain line, "we followed effects this far, for these reasons", gives the initiative something it can repeat to funders. It also gives a second agent a fixed edge to match, which helps two agents produce much the same page.

The second value is that it can show an initiative its own numbers more clearly. Repair Café International's waste figure is built from stated assumptions (R5). A page that lays those assumptions side by side with the initiative's own repair log hands it a sturdier figure to publish next year. That helps a repair network, a community energy scheme drawing on its sector's annual report (R1), or a land trust.

Third, even thin ownership evidence (R2) is useful when the page names which comparison is nearest. That tells a cooperative where the evidence runs out.

The first step for the agent: write the stopping rule, then list every figure the initiative publishes with its assumptions.

items.full:
Yes, in part. The wellbeing-budget publications I checked state where their *measurement* has gaps. I found no budget document that sets out which indirect effects were traced and where the tracing stopped, initiative by initiative.

- **New Zealand, Wellbeing Budget 2019 (Treasury).** The document says the Living Standards Framework Dashboard is a first version. It says further work is needed so that future versions improve "known gaps and limitations". It names the gaps as:
  - fuller expression of Te Ao Māori perspectives;
  - child wellbeing;
  - New Zealand cultural identity;
  - risk and resilience.

  This is an explicit statement of what the indicator set leaves out. It is not a statement of which effects of each initiative were followed or where the tracing stopped. The same text appears in the Budget Policy Statement 2019.
- **New Zealand, CBAx guidance (Treasury).** The guidance says every budget initiative needs a wellbeing analysis. It says that analysis applies even when CBAx isn't used and impacts aren't monetised. It also asks agencies to report monetised and unmonetised impacts and how robust they are. That comes closest to asking for a stated boundary, but it is guidance to agencies. I did not open the individual Budget submissions to see whether agencies actually follow it.
- **International Budget Partnership review (2020).** The review notes plans to refine the Treasury's Indicators Aotearoa New Zealand set to address data gaps in the environment. It also says wellbeing analysis in agency proposals varied in quality. I read this only through a search snippet.
- **OECD.** The OECD's own material on the future of its Well-being Dashboard (2019 draft) has a section headed "Limitations of the existing measures". That is about its indicator set, not about tracing effects.
- **Wales.** I searched the Well-being of Future Generations Act and Future Generations Report material. The results showed progress against national indicators. They did not show a statement of effects traced or where tracing stopped. I did not open the full report.

I did not search the Scottish, Icelandic, Finnish or Canadian budgets in any depth. A first search on Scotland's National Performance Framework was written but never ran, because the code failed before reaching it. I did not open the full 2019 Budget PDF, only extracts of it and the Treasury web pages.

For the note, the supportable claim is that governments publish known gaps in their indicators. I did not find any that publish an effect-tracing boundary for each initiative. That is the gap a whole-effect check would fill.

The sharpest risk I see is that a page with no score still gets read as a verdict, and it lands hardest on the smallest initiatives.

R1 shows a community energy sector with a yearly report, so a scheme like that gets a full page. A small repair group with no annual report, or a wellbeing budget where R8 found no statement of where tracing stopped, gets a page full of "could not be found". A funder skimming on a phone may read that as weakness rather than as missing paperwork. Yellow's honesty line could therefore count against exactly the bodies it was meant to help.

Second, the page names who carries the costs. In a community energy scheme that could mean fuel-poor households, and in a repair group it could mean the volunteer fixers. Neither group agreed to be on the page.

Third, a gap like R5's 70% assumption set beside a 63% log is fair to point out privately. Published, it would look like a charge.

Building on that: the risk of a page being read as a verdict has a sibling, which is that the agent will sound more certain than its sources allow.

White found no method fixing the number of steps (R4, R6), and the "one or two steps" bound has no source. The agent will still have to stop somewhere, and a stopping rule written in one confident sentence looks like a method when it is a choice. Two agents drawing the line in different places would return different pages. A funder comparing the closing blocks of two initiatives would then be comparing the agents' choices, not the initiatives.

Next, the "draft goes to the initiative alone" step assumes the initiative reads it with time to spare. A volunteer-run repair group may skim it, say yes, and forward it on. A draft with named households or fixers then travels without the agent's caveats. The risk is in how the page gets passed on.

Third, ownership comparison. R2 shows evidence that is resource-specific and thin on trusts and cooperatives. A page setting a cooperative beside "other arrangements" from different resources, such as forests or water, could suggest a lesson the evidence does not support. A board might then change how it is governed on the strength of it.

Fourth, the reversible small move. "Reversible" is the agent's guess. A reserved-capacity trial for fuel-poor households may be hard to withdraw once households have budgeted around it.

items.text:
One design answers several of Black's risks together: laundered figures, rival-written sources, thin paperwork read as weakness, and refusals with no next step. **The page is built from a source map drawn up before any tracing, and every line on the page carries a plain tag showing where it came from.**

1. **Map the sources.** The agent lists every document it will use: who wrote it, when, and whether it is the initiative's own, independent, or nothing more than an assumption.
2. **Tag every finding.** Each line on the page is marked "your records", "public, independent" or "our estimate". People are described by role, never by name.
3. **Say what would fill each gap.** Where a part has nothing behind it, the page says what would fill it instead of refusing.

Tried on three kinds of initiative:

- **A community energy scheme:** most lines would tag to its own reports and the sector report (R1).
- **A repair group:** the one-kilogram-per-object line tags "our estimate", and Restart's open data (R3) is named as what could replace it.
- **A wellbeing budget:** the gaps it already publishes (R8) become its "what would fill this" list.

First step tomorrow: draw source maps for those three from public documents and count how many lines end up as "our estimate".
asks: Does the Restart Project's open data give average weights per product category that could replace an assumed one kilogram per repaired object?

[Green · round 1 · second voice]

Building on the source-tagged page: add a **sorting rule that decides what the page may say at all**, so that the tag does real work instead of sitting as decoration.

**Three tags, three permissions.**
- "Your records" lines may state figures, but only beside the initiative's own stated assumption. Where its own log disagrees with its assumption, that goes in a private cover note, never on the shareable page.
- "Public, independent" lines may name a cost and the kind of party who carries it (a role, such as "households in fuel poverty"), with the source's own wording quoted in full, not clipped.
- "Our estimate" lines may only appear as a question or a range, never as a bare figure or a named harm. So a guessed cost to a group reads "worth asking whether...", which stops both softening and overstating.

**Why this helps.** Part 2 (who carries unpaid costs) and part 5 (loop gain, what could never be rebuilt) have no method behind them. Under this rule they can only be "our estimate", so they appear as questions by construction. Nobody has to trust the agent's judgement, because it is not allowed to give any there.

**Tried on three kinds.**
- A community energy scheme: bills and grid effects tag to the sector report (R1); effects on non-members stay questions.
- A repair group: the 63% log against a 70% assumption (R5) goes in the private note; the page says "measured figure available from your log".
- A wellbeing budget: its published gaps (R8) become the "our estimate" questions.

**First step tomorrow:** write the three-tag permission table on one screen, then apply it by hand to the Repair Café 2019 report (R5) and see which sentences survive.

Here is a different shape for the page: a growing list of open questions, not a finished account. Each year's page carries forward last year's questions and marks each one as answered (with its source), dropped by the initiative, or still open. The initiative decides the order and which questions matter most.

This gives the loop-gain question something checkable. Rather than asking the agent whether one turn makes the next easier, the yearly rerun counts questions closed with a source against new ones opened. A count is not proof, but both sides can see it, and it does not rest on the agent's opinion.

It also blunts the verdict risk. A list of open questions cannot be read as a score, and a trend line reflects what the initiative chose to close, since the carried-forward text is fixed wording the initiative edits, not the agent's fresh judgement.

Tried on three kinds of initiative:
- **Community energy:** a question about effects on non-members is closed by a sector report figure (R1), or carried forward.
- **Repair group:** "measured figure from your log?" stays open until outcomes are recorded, which is a plain prompt for the 63% versus 70% gap (R5).
- **Wellbeing budget:** the gaps New Zealand already publishes (R8) become the first year's open list.

First step tomorrow: turn the R8 gaps and the R5 repair figure into dated open questions, each with a named source or "none found".

Building on the carried-forward question list: **freeze the method alongside the questions**, so a yearly rerun compares the initiative with itself rather than one agent's choices with another's.

Each page ends with a short, fixed method block: the source map, the one-sentence stopping rule, and the three-tag permission table. Next year's agent must reuse that block word for word. If it wants to follow effects further or add a source, the change appears as a new open question ("should tracing now include X?") for the initiative to accept or decline. This answers three Black risks: a stopping rule that drifts between reruns, pages that compare agents rather than initiatives, and a requester generating many pages and keeping the most flattering one. A page whose method block differs from the agreed one is visibly not comparable.

Tried on three kinds:
- **Community energy:** the year-one block says tracing stopped at members' bills and the local grid. Effects on non-members enter only if the scheme accepts them.
- **Repair group:** the one-kilogram assumption (R5) stays tagged "our estimate" until Restart data (R3) is accepted into the block.
- **Wellbeing budget:** the ownership part can be marked "not applicable, by agreement", recorded once rather than forced every year.

First step tomorrow: write the year-one method block for the Repair Café 2019 report and test whether it fits in about ten lines on a phone.

[Green · round 2 · second voice]

Building on the frozen method block: add a **commissioning step that fixes who the page is for before any tracing starts**, because Black's risks about unauthorised pages, forwarding and the sole-record problem all begin at the request.

The agent first produces a one-screen "before we start" card, not the page. It states: who asked, in what role (stated, not verified), that the page is a draft for that body only, and which of three outputs it will return: a shareable page, a private cover note, or a plain "not enough to go on, here is what would change that". Every page carries a visible line: "requested by [role], not confirmed as speaking for the initiative". If a rival or outsider runs the service, that line travels with the page and is the first thing a reader sees.

The shareable page also gets a **correction slot**: a fixed last line saying "people described here by role may send a correction to the initiative, which can add it beside the line". The agent contacts nobody, but the page gives a route in.

Tried on three kinds:
- **Community energy:** a volunteer commissions it; the card shows the role, and the board sees that on the draft.
- **Repair group:** thin records give the "not enough yet" output, with Restart data (R3) named as the next input.
- **Wellbeing budget:** a council outsider runs it; the page is marked unconfirmed and carries no ownership section, by agreement.

First step tomorrow: draft the "before we start" card in six lines and test it on a request that arrives with no records at all.

Under the Green hat, this is an alternative to the agent drafting the page: **let the initiative draft its own five boxes, and the agent only tags them.**

1. **The initiative writes a first draft** of the five parts in its own words, from what it already knows.
2. **The agent tags each claim** as "supported by public sources", "only in the initiative's own records", or "no source found". It quotes the source line in full and attaches no judgement of its own.
3. **The agent lists what would test each untagged claim**, naming the public document or data set that could check it, such as Restart's open data (R3) for repair figures.
4. **The page is the initiative's draft with tags and a gap list added.** The agent's contribution is the tags and the gaps, not new findings.

This shifts the risks that Black raised about the agent's authorship. The agent cannot invent a harm, soften a cost or overstate one, because it writes none of the claims. It can still miss a source, so the tags carry the same "requested by" line and correction slot as before.

Tried on three kinds:

- **Repair group:** the 70% success assumption gets tagged "own records only", since the 2019 log shows 63% (R5).
- **Wellbeing budget:** the draft carries forward the gaps New Zealand already publishes (R8) as "no source found".

Building on the initiative-drafts, agent-tags idea, one gap remains: an initiative that writes its own five boxes can leave things out. So the agent adds a sixth box, **"Not in your draft"**. It lists only effects that public sources mention and the draft does not, and only as questions. That turns the round's pieces into one ordered procedure:

1. Fill in the before-we-start card.
2. Map the sources.
3. Take the initiative's five-box draft, or, if there is none, draft under the three-tag rules.
4. Tag each line and quote its source.
5. Add "Not in your draft".
6. Move any gaps between the initiative's own records and its stated assumptions into a private note.
7. Fix the method block.
8. Carry the open questions forward.

**The phone page, top to bottom:** the requested-by line, then one stopping sentence, then six boxes of three tagged lines each, then the open questions, then the method block, and last the correction slot.

**Tried on three kinds:**
- **Community energy:** "Not in your draft" asks about effects on non-members' bills, if the sector report (R1) mentions them.
- **Repair group:** it asks about effects on local paid repairers, if Restart (R3) covers them.
- **Wellbeing budget:** New Zealand's published gaps (R8) fill it.

**First step tomorrow:** lay out the page from the R5 report and check that it fits two phone screens.

[Green · round 3 · Sonnet]

Building on the eight-step procedure, one gap is left: a page that fits two screens can still run long, and a volunteer will answer "yes or no to being checked" before reading any of it. So add a **"what you get, what we need" opening card**, shown before any work begins, with a one-tap yes, no or "show me an example first".

The card has four lines:
- what the agent will do, in one sentence;
- what it needs from you, in a short list, with "nothing" as a valid answer;
- which of three outputs you will probably get (shareable page, private note, or "not enough yet");
- what it will not do: score, name people, or contact anyone.

The "show me an example" choice links to a finished page for a different kind of initiative, so a repair group sees a community energy page, and the reverse. Because the example is built from the public sector report (R1), it costs the initiative nothing and exposes nobody.

This also serves the steps already agreed. A "no" is recorded as a plain "declined", with no page made and nothing published, which answers the risk of unrequested pages being treated as a verdict on someone who said no.

Tried on three kinds:
- **Community energy:** the card says "nothing needed"; the agent starts from the sector report (R1).
- **Repair group:** the card asks for the repair log, and says that without it the output will be "not enough yet", naming Restart data (R3).
- **Wellbeing budget:** the card says ownership will be marked "not applicable, by agreement", and uses NZ's published gaps (R8).

First step tomorrow: write the four-line card and show it to the room as the page's very top line.

Sonnet's opening card leaves one gap: a published page stays in circulation after the request has changed. Green's answer is to make the page itself reversible, in the same spirit as the small move.

Each page carries a dated header: "Valid until [date, twelve months on]. Withdrawable by the requester at any time." The card offers a one-tap withdrawal. A withdrawn page keeps its address and shows one line: "Withdrawn by requester on [date]." Nothing is deleted silently, so anyone who reads the page later can see that it was pulled. Next year's rerun either reissues the page with fresh open questions or leaves the withdrawal standing.

Tried on three kinds:

- **Community energy:** the board withdraws a draft after a members' meeting that disputed one line. The replacement line stands, and the draft's text is not kept on the shareable address.

verdict.text:
The agent's steps, in order: (1) send a four-line card saying what you get and what we need, with yes, no, or show me an example; (2) record who asked and in what role; (3) list the sources before tracing anything; (4) write one sentence saying where tracing stops and why; (5) have the initiative draft its own boxes; (6) tag each claim as your records, public and independent, or our estimate; (7) list as questions what public sources mention and the draft omits; (8) name the nearest ownership comparison and one small trial, with how to undo it and who must agree.

The page: requested-by line, valid-until date, stopping sentence, six boxes, open questions, method block, correction slot. People appear by role only. Disagreements go in a private note.

The run changed the design from an agent that judges to one that tags and asks, and made the page itself withdrawable.

Still open: whether two agents produce the same page, whether a page with no score helps people decide, wellbeing-budget sources, and how to give rivers and future residents a say. The ownership evidence is thin, and nothing has been tried by hand.

Next check: two agents run the steps separately on one community energy scheme, one repair group and one wellbeing budget, then compare pages.
verdict.recommend: Rewrite the note so the agent tags and questions the initiative's own draft under a stated stopping sentence, replacing the "one or two steps" claim and the name "whole-effect check".

checkpoint.text:
# The whole-effect check: a service an AI agent can offer any initiative

_Forming (2026-11-21). A starting note for a six-hat run of the world computer. It follows [run-003](/world-computer?run=run-003), which worked only the first of seven draft steps for AI agents and left four unworked: tracing where hidden costs land, checking the whole effect of an initiative, comparing ownership arrangements, and proposing the small move that can be undone. This note folds those four into one service and asks the room to make it concrete. Nothing below has been checked. Every factual claim is unverified until a run checks it._

_Moved on 2026-11-21 by a [six-hat run](/world-computer?run=run-004): the agent no longer judges an initiative; it tags and questions the initiative's own draft under a stated stopping sentence, and the page itself can be withdrawn._

---

## Where this starts

Tom Cassidy's framing, given at a conference in Bologna on 21 November 2026, put in this note's words except where quoted:

- **The measure is possibility.** Some arrangements of the same matter open more possibilities than others. The atoms in a phone were all in the ground; they were dug up and assembled, and the assembled phone lets its holder do things the ore never could. (The idea of counting how much assembling a thing took comes from the chemist Lee Cronin's Assembly Theory.) So the question to ask of any move is which way it pushes the set of futures that people and living systems can still reach.
- **The aim, in his words:** "More possibilities for all and less to none".
- **The DNA economy.** A circular economy keeps materials going round at a steady level. Tom's extension is a loop that gains each time round, the way living things reuse the same atoms while what they can do keeps growing: each turn of the loop leaves behind know-how, tools or trust that makes the next turn open more. What grows is the pattern, not the amount of material or energy used.
- **Forward-facing and blame-agnostic.** The present state is the starting point. History is information about where everyone now stands, never a debt.
- **Ownership is an arrangement.** Who owns a thing is one option among several that can be compared by the same question.
- **It plays nicely with every other initiative.** Nobody has to be wrong. The check below is offered as a service to people already doing the work.

## The service, as first drafted

An initiative (a community energy scheme, a repair and reuse network, a wellbeing budget, a land trust, a company's product line) asks: *what is the whole effect of what we are doing?* An AI agent, working only from public information and what the initiative itself hands over, contacting nobody else, returns one page. The page has five parts.

1. **What it opens, for whom, how soon.** The possibilities the initiative creates, and for which people and living systems.
2. **Where the costs that are not in the price land.** Each cost the initiative does not pay itself, followed to whoever carries it: neighbours, non-members, another place, a later year, a river, a soil.
3. **Indirect effects.** What changes one or two steps away: what people stop doing, what the saved money gets spent on, who loses custom, what gets easier or harder for the next initiative.
4. **The arrangement.** Who owns and decides now, set beside two or three other arrangements that exist somewhere for the same kind of thing (private, public, commons, trust, shared), and which way each has pushed where it was tried.
5. **The small move that can be undone.** One change the initiative could try that would open more for those currently getting less, and how to reverse it if it fails. Plus: does each turn of the initiative make its next turn easier (does the loop gain), and is anything at risk that could never be rebuilt?

The page gives no score and no verdict on the initiative. It ends in questions the initiative can answer better than the agent can.

## The service, as the run left it

The run kept the five questions but changed who answers them. In the first draft the agent writes claims about the initiative. The run found that this makes the page read as a verdict, lets weak figures look checked, and describes people who never spoke. In the revised design the initiative writes its own answers and the agent tags them and asks questions. The run also recommends dropping the name "whole-effect check", because no method traces a whole effect and a funder skimming the title may take the page as the full picture. A new name has not been chosen.

**The agent's steps, in order.** Two agents given the same initiative should follow the same steps.

1. **Send a four-line card**, saying what the initiative gets and what the agent needs, with one-tap answers: yes, no, or "show me an example first". The example is a finished page for a different kind of initiative, which could be built from a public sector report such as Community Energy England's annual [State of the Sector report](https://communityenergyengland.org/publications/state-of-the-sector-2025/). That report has been produced since 2017, and the latest is dated 17 September 2025 ([series page](https://communityenergyengland.org/state-of-the-sector/)). A "no" is recorded as "declined" and no page is made.
2. **Record who asked and in what role.** The agent cannot verify this because it contacts nobody, so the page carries a visible line: "Requested by [role], not confirmed as speaking for the initiative." The requester chooses one of three outputs: a shareable page, a private cover note, or "not enough to go on". A "not enough to go on" reply must say what the agent would need, so that it is a next step and not a bare refusal.
3. **List the sources before tracing anything.** This means public documents and records handed over, each marked as the initiative's own, public and independent, or neither, with its date. For repair networks, for example, Repair Café International publishes annual reports, a starter kit and a map of groups ([annual reports](https://www.repaircafe.org/en/category/annual-report/)). The Restart Project publishes annual reports, repair data and open reference data on the impact of repairs ([FAQ and data](https://therestartproject.org/faq/)). No equivalent list was confirmed for wellbeing budgets.
4. **Write one sentence saying where tracing stops and why.** This replaces the first draft's "one or two steps away", which has no source. Established methods set no fixed number of steps. ISO 14044 for life-cycle assessment requires a study to state its cut-off criteria and test how they affect the result ([ISO 14044:2006](https://archive.org/stream/gov.in.is.iso.14044.2006/is.iso.14044.2006_djvu.txt)). The social return on investment guide and the EU Better Regulation Toolbox, chapter 8, rely on materiality and proportionality, and the SROI guide also allows for effects fading over time ([SROI guide, 2009](https://ifcsia.org/wp-content/uploads/pdf/publications/Measuring-Value-A-Guide-to-Social-Return-on-Investment.pdf); [EU Toolbox ch. 8, 2023](https://commission.europa.eu/system/files/2023-09/BRT-2023-Chapter%208-Methodologies%20for%20analysing%20impacts%20in%20IAs%20evaluations%20and%20fitness%20checks_0.pdf)). Supply-chain methods that cut off at a chosen number of tiers were not checked.
5. **Have the initiative draft its own boxes**, answering the five questions in its own words.
6. **Tag each claim** in the draft as "your records", "public and independent", or "our estimate", quoting any public source in full. Each tag limits what the page may say:
   - A "your records" figure may appear only beside the initiative's own stated assumption.
   - A "public and independent" cost may be stated at the level of a role, with the source quoted.
   - An "our estimate" may appear only as a question or a range.

   For example, Repair Café International's figure of about 420,000 kg of waste prevented in 2019 comes from 2,000 cafés × 12 meetings × 25 objects × 70% success × an assumed 1 kg per object, while its own 2019 repair log showed 63% success ([news item](https://www.repaircafe.org/en/repair-cafes-prevent-420000-kilos-of-waste-in-2019/); [2019 summary report](https://www.repaircafe.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Annual_report_2019_Summary_ENGLISH_12_2020-3.pdf)). The page would set that figure beside its assumptions. The agent's disagreements with the draft go in a private note to the requester, not on the page.
7. **List as questions** the effects that public sources mention and the draft omits. This becomes the sixth box, "Not in your draft".
8. **Name the nearest ownership comparison and one small trial**, saying how the trial would be undone and who must agree to it. Evidence on ownership is thin. It includes a review of 91 commons studies (Cox et al., 2010), comparisons of forest commons (Chhatre and Agrawal) and reviews of water privatisation (for example Araral) ([Cox et al.](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/992c/afca81f665d9279e48f741611b78c6eb3110.pdf); [review](https://dx.doi.org/10.3390/su9071287)). It is specific to each resource and says little about trusts and cooperatives. No single source compares all five arrangements across resources. The page should therefore say where the evidence runs out rather than draw a lesson from it. For some initiatives, such as a publicly held wellbeing budget, the comparison may not fit at all, and the page should say so.

**The page, laid out for a phone:**

- a requested-by line
- a valid-until date, twelve months on, with "withdrawable by the requester at any time"
- the stopping sentence
- six boxes: the initiative's five, tagged, plus "Not in your draft"
- open questions
- a method block, holding the source list, the stopping sentence and the tag rules
- a correction slot for anyone the page describes

People appear by role only. A withdrawn page keeps its address and shows only "Withdrawn by requester on [date]". A page made for someone outside the initiative expires after a year unless the initiative adopts it.

**Yearly reruns.** The method block is reused word for word each year. Any change to it is raised as an open question that the initiative can accept or decline. This way the trend compares the initiative with itself, not one agent's choices with another's. The run proposed one firmer answer to "does the loop gain": count the open questions closed with a source each year against the new ones opened. This is untested. No method was found for "could anything never be rebuilt", so the page asks it only as a question.

## Why an initiative might want it

Published reports rarely state where their tracing stopped. The run found no community energy or repair report on social return that states its cut-off rule in one plain sentence. The nearest was the generic NEF guide, and a Repair Café Wales report could not be opened in full ([NEF guide](https://new-economicsf.files.svdcdn.com/production/files/aff3779953c5b88d53_cpm6v3v71.pdf); [Repair Café Wales](https://cydinnovation.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Repair-Cafe-FINAL-06-26.pdf)). New Zealand's Wellbeing Budget 2019 names the gaps in its dashboard, and Treasury's CBAx guidance asks for unmonetised impacts to be reported. However, no wellbeing-budget publication was found that says which indirect effects were traced and where tracing stopped ([Wellbeing Budget 2019](https://www.treasury.govt.nz/publications/wellbeing-budget/wellbeing-budget-2019); [CBAx guide](https://www.treasury.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2018-09/cbax-guide-sep18.pdf)).

The page could offer an initiative four things:

- a stopping sentence it can repeat to funders
- sturdier figures, such as a measured weight per object from open repair data in place of an assumed one kilogram
- an honest "what could not be found" line
- a trend series from cheap yearly reruns

A shared method block would also let funders compare how far different kinds of initiative traced, not how well each told its story. None of this has been tried.

## Risks the design must carry

These are risks to the design, not charges against anyone.

- **Read as a verdict.** A page with no score may still be read as a verdict. Gaps in the record land hardest on small, thinly documented bodies, such as a repair group with no annual report.
- **Refusing those who most need it.** A minimum number of sources would either turn away the bodies that most need an outside view or become a reassuring count with no benchmark behind it.
- **Selective records.** The initiative controls what it hands over, so incomplete logs or only the good months can make a page look balanced.
- **Uncheckable sources.** Public sources may be old, partial or written by rivals, and the agent may invent a plausible source. Quoting sources in full moves the checking to a time-poor reader on a phone.
- **Leaning either way.** The blame-agnostic tone may push the agent to soften a cost that documents state plainly. Fear of flattering may push it to overstate a cost it can only guess at.
- **People who never spoke.** Because the agent contacts nobody, those who carry costs are described from documents only. The SROI guide treats talking to those affected as what gives such work credibility. No consent rule can reach rivers, soils or future residents.
- **Caveats lost in forwarding.** A busy volunteer may approve and forward a draft, and the caveats get lost on the way.
- **Uninvited pages.** A rival or sceptical neighbour may commission a page the initiative never asked for. Because pages cost almost nothing, someone could also make many and publish the most flattering.
- **Trials that are hard to undo.** A trial called reversible may be hard to withdraw once households have budgeted around it, for example reserved capacity for fuel-poor households. A funder may also treat "can be undone" as a reason to stop early.
- **Unanswered questions.** Questions may go unanswered by an unstaffed body, leaving the page as the only account.

## What the run is asked to settle

- The exact steps the agent takes for each part, in order, so that a different agent given the same initiative would produce much the same page. *(Steps drafted above. Whether two agents match is untested.)*
- What the agent must be handed, and what it can find for itself. *(Partly settled by steps 3 and 5.)*
- How "one or two steps away" is bounded, so that the tracing stops somewhere. *(Replaced by the stopping sentence in step 4.)*
- What stops the page doing harm: to the initiative, to people named in it, to those left out of it. *(Partly settled by role-only naming, private disagreements, withdrawal, expiry and the correction slot. Those left out remain open.)*
- Whether this is worth more to an initiative than what it already does for itself. *(Untested.)*

## What is not known

- Whether indirect effects can be traced reliably from public information at all.
- Whether a page with no score is usable by anyone who has to make a decision.
- Whether the "does the loop gain" question can be answered with anything firmer than opinion. Counting questions closed against questions opened is one untested candidate.
- Whether two agents following the same steps produce the same page.
- What a single community energy scheme or repair group publishes, and what public documents exist for wellbeing budgets.
- How to give rivers, soils and future residents a say on a page that contacts nobody.
- Whether the Bologna and Lee Cronin attributions are accurate. The run did not check them.
- Nothing in the procedure has yet been tried by hand.

## Next check

Two agents run the eight steps separately on the same three initiatives: one community energy scheme, one repair group and one wellbeing budget. They then compare their pages line by line, noting where the stopping sentence, the tags and the "Not in your draft" questions differ.

better: Turns the first draft's five headings into eight ordered steps, a page layout and a concrete next check (two agents, three initiatives, line-by-line comparison).

Replaces the unsourced "one or two steps away" with a stated stopping sentence, grounded in ISO 14044, the SROI guide and the EU Toolbox, and admits that tier-based supply-chain methods were not checked.
Tag rules limit what each kind of claim may say, and the Repair Café example works: 2,000 × 12 × 25 × 70% × 1 kg does equal 420,000 kg, and the conflicting 63% logged success rate is disclosed.
Adds options for several parties: decline, "show me an example first", three output types, withdrawal, twelve-month expiry, a correction slot for anyone described, and role-only naming.
The ownership-evidence caveat is carried into step 8 in substance: evidence is thin, resource-specific, has no five-way comparison, and may not fit at all.
The risks section is specific and candid about selective records, invented sources, uninvited pages, hard-to-undo trials and people who never spoke.
"What is not known" grows honestly, adding the unchecked Bologna and Cronin attributions and "nothing has been tried by hand".
Each item under "asked to settle" is annotated as settled, partly settled or untested, with no claim of closure.
worse: Step 5 moves the drafting burden onto the initiative. An unstaffed body that could simply ask for a page under the original must now write five boxes, and the risks list does not name this as a cost of the redesign.
The agent's disagreements with the draft go only in a private note to the requester. Funders, neighbours and cost-bearers reading the page lose the independent view the original implied.

Uninvited pages are flagged as a risk yet provided for ("a page made for someone outside the initiative"). The steps do not say who drafts the boxes in that case, since step 5 assumes the initiative does.
The header still says "Nothing below has been checked" beside a dozen sourced claims, and "What the run is asked to settle" keeps a heading written for a run that has now happened.
The "contacting nobody" premise sits unreconciled with sending a card and requiring the initiative to draft.
The run recommends dropping the name "whole-effect check", but the title keeps it and offers no interim name.
The note is much longer and keeps the superseded first draft in full, so a reader must work out which design is current.
unsupported: The claim that the SROI guide treats talking to those affected as what gives such work credibility has no pinpoint citation where it is made, though the guide is linked elsewhere.
Chhatre and Agrawal and Araral are named, but the only link offered is a vaguely labelled "review" DOI, so it is unclear which source supports which claim.
The "NEF guide" and the "nef / SROI Network guide" are listed as separate sources but look like the same document, which overstates the evidence base.
The Repair Café Wales link carries a 2026/06 path and could not be opened in full. This is honestly flagged, but it bears no weight as evidence.
"The run found no community energy or repair report that states its cut-off rule" is a negative finding with no stated search scope.
The four benefits to an initiative and the funder-comparison benefit are assertions, though the note does mark them "none of this has been tried".
critic.verdict: The revision is clearly better on balance: it makes the service concrete, sources or openly flags its new claims, keeps the original caveats in substance and adds exit and correction options for most parties. It passes with reservations, because the shift to initiative-drafted boxes and private-only agent disagreements narrows what low-capacity initiatives and outside readers get, and the note does not own that trade-off.
